intro: Weekly contribution margin by line and consolidated (accrual: revenue and costs in the week the order ships; ad spend in the week it is incurred)

Contribution margin = revenue - refunds & processing - COGS of units shipped - fulfillment - ad spend. Opex and operating profit are shown at the bottom. This is the P&L view; tab 7 is the cash view (card float, PayPal reserve, inventory bought ahead).
Ramp scenarios for your three questions - simulated with a Python twin of this workbook (static values; they do not recalculate)

Each scenario re-runs the whole model (same inputs as tab 1 except the levers named). 'Peak cash pull' for Haskap/AVIA = the largest gap between cash WITH the line and cash WITHOUT it, i.e. the incremental funding that line needs. All scenarios here use pay-as-you-go ad payment (lag 0) unless the row says otherwise, so they show true cash need without card float.

tables.read: at the 0.9x base, cacao alone still self-funds on pay-as-you-go as long as the second leg to $150K/day is not taken before W46 (Nov 9): straight to $150K on Nov 1 dips to about -$170K in mid-November; W46 is break-even; W48 (the base) bottoms at ~$140K; holding at $100K/day keeps ~$610K. With the Amex float and a $1M limit every speed stays above ~$550K. At 1.0x or 1.1x there is no constraint. So the pace is set by ROAS and the card limit, not by the $450K.

tables.read: at 0.75x a $1M/month Haskap line needs ~$650-730K of incremental cash at its deepest point (mid-Feb to mid-Mar) and is only back to even at the end of June; at 0.8x the pull is ~$490-600K and it is clearly accretive by late May; at 0.7x it is still ~$340-510K underwater on Jun 30. Ramping slower lowers the peak only modestly because spend keeps compounding. This assumes Haskap cohorts rebill exactly like cacao (45% / 70%) - the biggest unknown.

tables.read: at 0.7x, $3M/month by May 1 needs ~$2.8M of cash (peak in late May, after the last ramp weeks' spend lands and before their cycle-1 rebills) and is still ~$2.4M underwater on Jun 30. Each 0.1x of ROAS is worth ~$0.7-1.1M of peak funding: 0.8x = ~$1.6M, 0.9x = ~$0.95M and cash-positive by late May. On this playbook a 0.7x line pays back in ~5 cycles (140 days): every $1 of spend returns ~$1.10 of contribution over 168 days, so the line is profitable but the ramp needs the cash up front. Also assumes AVIA cohorts rebill like cacao.

tables.read: at 0.9x cacao the combined plan does NOT self-fund on pay-as-you-go - it bottoms at about -$640K in the week of Dec 21 (cacao ramping to $150K while Haskap and AVIA both burn). The Amex float with a $1M limit just clears it (~$80K low); a $2.5M limit removes the problem. Without that float the cheapest fixes are sequencing, not cash: start AVIA in January (-$120K low, or +$600K with a $1M card), start both new lines in January (+$55K low with no float at all), or hold cacao at $100K/day until the new lines are through their first rebill cycle (+$210K low). By April every variant is cash-positive and growing, and cacao's rebill base funds AVIA's May target from operating cash.
